problem_statement: Regression task: predict a continuous 'Prompt Quality Score' (0–10) from raw prompt text. Features are extracted via sentence-transformer embeddings (semantic density) plus hand-crafted lexical/structural statistics. A RandomForestRegressor is the primary estimator; Ridge regression is used as a linear baseline. The model enables real-time quality inference via FastAPI so users receive instant feedback before sending prompts to expensive LLM APIs.
result_analysis: The RandomForestRegressor achieved an R² of 0.9503 on the held-out test set, which is classified as 'Excellent' performance. The RMSE of 0.5365 indicates that predictions deviate by approximately 0.54 quality points on average — acceptable given a 0-10 scale. The baseline Ridge model attained R²=0.9675, confirming that the non-linear Random Forest captures richer interaction patterns from the embedding space. Cross-validation R² (0.9402 ± 0.0061) demonstrates model stability without significant overfitting.

conclusion.findings: A RandomForestRegressor trained on sentence-transformer embeddings (384-dim) combined with 9 hand-crafted lexical features achieved R²=0.9503 on unseen test data, demonstrating that prompt quality is predictable from structural and semantic text cues alone.
conclusion.limitations: 1. The dataset is synthetic; real-world prompt ratings collected from human annotators would improve generalisation. 2. The quality score heuristic is rule-based, which may not fully capture subjective prompt 'clarity'. 3. The model does not account for domain-specific prompt patterns (e.g., coding vs. creative writing prompts may have different quality signals).
conclusion.future_improvements: 1. Replace synthetic labels with RLHF-style human preference data. 2. Fine-tune the embedding model end-to-end (not just as a frozen encoder). 3. Add a SHAP explainer endpoint to surface per-token feature attributions. 4. Implement online learning so the model improves from user feedback. 5. Extend to multi-output regression: predict both quality and expected LLM response quality simultaneously.
